claim: Trophic deprivation (TD) of mouse sensory neurons causes a rapid disassembly of the axonal MPS.
source: We show that trophic deprivation (TD) of mouse sensory neurons causes a rapid disassembly of the axonal MPS, which occurs prior to protein loss and independently of caspase activation.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: MPS disassembly occurs prior to protein loss during trophic deprivation.
source: We show that trophic deprivation (TD) of mouse sensory neurons causes a rapid disassembly of the axonal MPS, which occurs prior to protein loss and independently of caspase activation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by data in Figure 2F showing protein levels remain constant during early TD.

claim: MPS disassembly occurs independently of caspase activation during trophic deprivation.
source: We show that trophic deprivation (TD) of mouse sensory neurons causes a rapid disassembly of the axonal MPS, which occurs prior to protein loss and independently of caspase activation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by experiments with Bcl-xL overexpression and Bax knockout shown in Figure 2.

claim: Actin destabilization initiates TD-related retrograde signaling needed for degeneration.
source: Actin destabilization initiates TD-related retrograde signaling needed for degeneration; actin stabilization prevents MPS disassembly and retrograde signaling during TD.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by latrunculin A experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Actin stabilization prevents MPS disassembly during TD.
source: Actin destabilization initiates TD-related retrograde signaling needed for degeneration; actin stabilization prevents MPS disassembly and retrograde signaling during TD.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by Jasplakinolide experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Actin stabilization prevents retrograde signaling during TD.
source: Actin destabilization initiates TD-related retrograde signaling needed for degeneration; actin stabilization prevents MPS disassembly and retrograde signaling during TD.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by Jasplakinolide experiments showing reduced c-Jun phosphorylation in Figure 4.

claim: Depletion of βII-spectrin suppresses retrograde signaling during trophic deprivation.
source: Depletion of βII-spectrin, a key component of the MPS, suppresses retrograde signaling and protects axons against degeneration.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by shRNA and knockout experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Depletion of βII-spectrin protects axons against degeneration.
source: Depletion of βII-spectrin, a key component of the MPS, suppresses retrograde signaling and protects axons against degeneration.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by axon degeneration assays shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: βII-spectrin is a key component of the MPS.
source: Depletion of βII-spectrin, a key component of the MPS, suppresses retrograde signaling and protects axons against degeneration.
evidence: The abstract states this, which is established knowledge from prior studies cited in the introduction.

claim: Sensory axons of the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) compete for limited quantities of target-derived neurotrophins that promote axon survival during development.
source: This is exemplified in the development of the peripheral nervous system where sensory axons of the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) compete for limited quantities of target-derived neurotrophins that promote axon survival.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Luo and O'Leary, 2005 and Schuldiner and Yaron, 2015.

claim: Axons that receive sufficient trophic support survive and mature, whereas axons that are insufficiently supported by neurotrophins degenerate.
source: Axons that receive sufficient trophic support survive and mature, whereas axons that are insufficiently supported by neurotrophins degenerate (Luo and O'Leary, 2005; Schuldiner and Yaron, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Luo and O'Leary, 2005 and Schuldiner and Yaron, 2015.

claim: Upon TD, the axon first generates a retrograde signal to the neuronal cell body.
source: Upon TD, the axon first generates a retrograde signal to the neuronal cell body; next, this retrograde signal initiates a pro-degenerative transcriptional response in the cell body; finally, the cell body generates an anterograde signal that propagates to the axon and gates the activation of a latent apoptotic cascade within the axon (Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016; Maor-Nof et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016; Maor-Nof et al., 2016.

claim: The retrograde signal initiates a pro-degenerative transcriptional response in the cell body during TD.
source: Upon TD, the axon first generates a retrograde signal to the neuronal cell body; next, this retrograde signal initiates a pro-degenerative transcriptional response in the cell body; finally, the cell body generates an anterograde signal that propagates to the axon and gates the activation of a latent apoptotic cascade within the axon (Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016; Maor-Nof et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016; Maor-Nof et al., 2016.

claim: The cell body generates an anterograde signal that propagates to the axon and gates the activation of a latent apoptotic cascade within the axon during TD.
source: Upon TD, the axon first generates a retrograde signal to the neuronal cell body; next, this retrograde signal initiates a pro-degenerative transcriptional response in the cell body; finally, the cell body generates an anterograde signal that propagates to the axon and gates the activation of a latent apoptotic cascade within the axon (Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016; Maor-Nof et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016; Maor-Nof et al., 2016.

claim: Actin, spectrin and associated molecules form a Membrane-associated Periodic Skeleton (MPS) in axons.
source: It has been shown recently that actin, spectrin and associated molecules form a Membrane-associated Periodic Skeleton (MPS) in axons (Xu et al., 2013), as well as some dendrites (Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017), of neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017.

claim: The MPS is found in some dendrites of neurons.
source: It has been shown recently that actin, spectrin and associated molecules form a Membrane-associated Periodic Skeleton (MPS) in axons (Xu et al., 2013), as well as some dendrites (Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017), of neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017.

claim: The neuronal MPS contains molecules homologous to the components of the erythrocyte membrane skeleton.
source: The neuronal MPS contains molecules homologous to the components of the erythrocyte membrane skeleton (Bennett and Baines, 2001) but adopts a different ultrastructural organization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Bennett and Baines, 2001.

claim: The neuronal MPS adopts a different ultrastructural organization than the erythrocyte membrane skeleton.
source: The neuronal MPS contains molecules homologous to the components of the erythrocyte membrane skeleton (Bennett and Baines, 2001) but adopts a different ultrastructural organization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Bennett and Baines, 2001 and prior structural studies.

claim: In the MPS, actin is arranged into ring-like structures.
source: In the MPS, actin is arranged into ring-like structures, and these actin rings are connected by heterotetramers of α- and β-spectrin, forming a quasi-one-dimensional (1D) periodic lattice structure underneath the plasma membrane (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Actin rings in the MPS are connected by heterotetramers of α- and β-spectrin.
source: In the MPS, actin is arranged into ring-like structures, and these actin rings are connected by heterotetramers of α- and β-spectrin, forming a quasi-one-dimensional (1D) periodic lattice structure underneath the plasma membrane (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: The MPS forms a quasi-one-dimensional (1D) periodic lattice structure underneath the plasma membrane.
source: In the MPS, actin is arranged into ring-like structures, and these actin rings are connected by heterotetramers of α- and β-spectrin, forming a quasi-one-dimensional (1D) periodic lattice structure underneath the plasma membrane (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: The MPS is assembled early during axon development.
source: The MPS is assembled early during axon development, forming initially in the axonal region proximal to the cell body and then propagating outward to span the entire axonal shaft (Zhong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zhong et al., 2014.

claim: The MPS forms initially in the axonal region proximal to the cell body and then propagates outward to span the entire axonal shaft.
source: The MPS is assembled early during axon development, forming initially in the axonal region proximal to the cell body and then propagating outward to span the entire axonal shaft (Zhong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zhong et al., 2014.

claim: The MPS is found in dendrites with lower propensity and developmental rate than in axons.
source: The MPS is also found in dendrites (Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015) but with lower propensity and developmental rate than in axons (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017.

claim: The MPS is present in all neuronal types examined in the central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: The MPS is present in all neuronal types examined in the central and peripheral nervous systems (D'Este et al., 2016; He et al., 2016) and is evolutionally conserved across diverse species ranging from Caenorhabditis elegans to Homo sapiens (He et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to D'Este et al., 2016; He et al., 2016.

claim: The MPS is evolutionally conserved across diverse species ranging from Caenorhabditis elegans to Homo sapiens.
source: The MPS is present in all neuronal types examined in the central and peripheral nervous systems (D'Este et al., 2016; He et al., 2016) and is evolutionally conserved across diverse species ranging from Caenorhabditis elegans to Homo sapiens (He et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to He et al., 2016.

claim: Genetic perturbations of components of the MPS suggest its importance in stability and survival of axons under mechanical stress.
source: Genetic perturbations of components of the MPS suggest its importance in processes such as stability and survival of axons under mechanical stress (Hammarlund et al., 2007), touch sensation (Krieg et al., 2014), the formation of axon initial segments (AIS) and nodes of Ranvier (Voas et al., 2007; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2017a), and the maintenance of axon morphology (Leite et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hammarlund et al., 2007.

claim: Genetic perturbations of components of the MPS suggest its importance in touch sensation.
source: Genetic perturbations of components of the MPS suggest its importance in processes such as stability and survival of axons under mechanical stress (Hammarlund et al., 2007), touch sensation (Krieg et al., 2014), the formation of axon initial segments (AIS) and nodes of Ranvier (Voas et al., 2007; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2017a), and the maintenance of axon morphology (Leite et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Krieg et al., 2014.

claim: Genetic perturbations of components of the MPS suggest its importance in the formation of axon initial segments (AIS) and nodes of Ranvier.
source: Genetic perturbations of components of the MPS suggest its importance in processes such as stability and survival of axons under mechanical stress (Hammarlund et al., 2007), touch sensation (Krieg et al., 2014), the formation of axon initial segments (AIS) and nodes of Ranvier (Voas et al., 2007; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2017a), and the maintenance of axon morphology (Leite et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Voas et al., 2007; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2017a.

claim: Genetic perturbations of components of the MPS suggest its importance in the maintenance of axon morphology.
source: Genetic perturbations of components of the MPS suggest its importance in processes such as stability and survival of axons under mechanical stress (Hammarlund et al., 2007), touch sensation (Krieg et al., 2014), the formation of axon initial segments (AIS) and nodes of Ranvier (Voas et al., 2007; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2017a), and the maintenance of axon morphology (Leite et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Leite et al., 2016.

claim: The MPS is important for organizing some membrane proteins, such as ion channels and adhesion molecules.
source: The MPS is also found to be important for organizing some membrane proteins, such as ion channels and adhesion molecules (Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; D'Este et al., 2017), membrane filtering at the AIS (Albrecht et al., 2016), and maintenance of axonal microtubules (Qu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; D'Este et al., 2017.

claim: The MPS is important for membrane filtering at the AIS.
source: The MPS is also found to be important for organizing some membrane proteins, such as ion channels and adhesion molecules (Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; D'Este et al., 2017), membrane filtering at the AIS (Albrecht et al., 2016), and maintenance of axonal microtubules (Qu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Albrecht et al., 2016.

claim: The MPS is important for maintenance of axonal microtubules.
source: The MPS is also found to be important for organizing some membrane proteins, such as ion channels and adhesion molecules (Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; D'Este et al., 2017), membrane filtering at the AIS (Albrecht et al., 2016), and maintenance of axonal microtubules (Qu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Qu et al., 2017.

claim: Disruption of the MPS causes widespread neurodegeneration and a variety of neurological impairments.
source: Disruption of the MPS causes widespread neurodegeneration and a variety of neurological impairments (Huang et al., 2017a; Huang et al., 2017b) and has been implicated in neuronal toxicity in Parkinson's disease (Ordonez et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2017a; Huang et al., 2017b.

claim: The MPS has been implicated in neuronal toxicity in Parkinson's disease.
source: Disruption of the MPS causes widespread neurodegeneration and a variety of neurological impairments (Huang et al., 2017a; Huang et al., 2017b) and has been implicated in neuronal toxicity in Parkinson's disease (Ordonez et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ordonez et al., 2018.

claim: MPS disassembly during TD was also reported independently by Unsain et al., 2018.
source: We found that trophic deprivation (TD) induced a rapid disassembly of the MPS, an observation also reported independently (Unsain et al., 2018) while our paper was in preparation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Unsain et al., 2018.

claim: Significant disruption of MPS occurs within 6 hr of TD.
source: To our surprise, we observed significant disruption of MPS within 6 hr of TD when there was neither obvious axon fragmentation nor detectable increase in immunoreactivity for cleaved (activated) Caspase-3 (Figure 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Within 6 hr of TD, there is no obvious axon fragmentation.
source: To our surprise, we observed significant disruption of MPS within 6 hr of TD when there was neither obvious axon fragmentation nor detectable increase in immunoreactivity for cleaved (activated) Caspase-3 (Figure 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Within 6 hr of TD, there is no detectable increase in immunoreactivity for cleaved (activated) Caspase-3.
source: To our surprise, we observed significant disruption of MPS within 6 hr of TD when there was neither obvious axon fragmentation nor detectable increase in immunoreactivity for cleaved (activated) Caspase-3 (Figure 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Genetic deletion of pro-apoptotic proteins Bax, Caspase-9, and Caspase-3 each potently protects axons from degeneration.
source: Genetic deletion of pro-apoptotic proteins Bax, Caspase-9, and Caspase-3 each potently protects axons from degeneration (Simon et al., 2012; Cusack et al., 2013; Unsain et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Simon et al., 2012; Cusack et al., 2013; Unsain et al., 2013.

claim: Caspase-3 cleaves Calpastatin, an endogenous inhibitor of Calpains, to promote degeneration.
source: To promote degeneration, Caspase-3 cleaves a number of key substrates including Calpastatin, an endogenous inhibitor of Calpains.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge of caspase substrates.

claim: Caspases and Calpains execute axon degeneration by cleaving many proteins including cytoskeleton components.
source: Together, Caspases and Calpains execute axon degeneration by cleaving many proteins including cytoskeleton components (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2013.

claim: Caspase activation precedes observable signs of degeneration such as blebbing of the plasma membrane and fragmentation of the microtubule network.
source: Caspase activation is thought to be one of the early steps of axon degeneration as it precedes observable signs of degeneration such as blebbing of the plasma membrane and fragmentation of the microtubule network (Schoenmann et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schoenmann et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2012.

claim: Overexpression of Bcl-xL did not inhibit the early disruption of the MPS upon TD.
source: Notably, we found that overexpression of Bcl-xL did not inhibit the early disruption of the MPS upon TD (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Bcl-xL overexpression potently blocks axon degeneration following TD.
source: Bcl-xL inhibits Bax, which is in turn required to activate effector Caspases, and it has been shown that the overexpression of Bcl-xL potently blocks axon degeneration following TD (Figure 2A) (Vohra et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2A and citations to Vohra et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2016.

claim: MPS disassembly proceeded normally in Bax-knockout axons.
source: Consistent with our Bcl-xL overexpression data, MPS disassembly proceeded normally in Bax-knockout axons (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This statement is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Bax-knockout axons are protected from degeneration following TD.
source: In parallel, we also measured changes in the MPS in axons from Bax-knockout mice (Knudson et al., 1995), which are similarly protected from degeneration following TD (Figure 2A) (Nikolaev et al., 2009; Simon et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2A and citations to Nikolaev et al., 2009; Simon et al., 2012.

claim: The average fluorescence intensity of βII spectrin in axon regions was unchanged during the first 12 hr of TD.
source: Notably, while TD causes a substantial decrease in MPS periodicity, the average fluorescence intensity of βII spectrin in these axon regions was unchanged during the first 12 hr of TD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the disassembly of the MPS was not a result of the reduced abundance of its protein components during TD.
evidence: This statement is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall levels of αII spectrin, βII spectrin and actin in axons remained constant during the first 9 hr of TD.
source: The overall levels of αII spectrin, βII spectrin and actin in axons remained constant during the first 9 hr of TD when MPS disassembly already started (Figure 2F), and only at later time points did we observe cleavage of αII spectrin, reflective of a Caspase-dependent cleavage of this protein during TD (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Cleavage of αII spectrin occurs at later time points during TD and is reflective of Caspase-dependent cleavage.
source: The overall levels of αII spectrin, βII spectrin and actin in axons remained constant during the first 9 hr of TD when MPS disassembly already started (Figure 2F), and only at later time points did we observe cleavage of αII spectrin, reflective of a Caspase-dependent cleavage of this protein during TD (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F and citation to Yang et al., 2013.

claim: Late cleavage of αII spectrin was blocked by expression of Bcl-xL.
source: Indeed, this late cleavage of αII spectrin was blocked by expression of Bcl-xL.
evidence: This statement is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Numerous de novo phosphorylations were detected on αII-spectrin, βII-spectrin, α-adducin, β−adducin and γ-adducin proteins during TD.
source: As part of an ongoing, large-scale, unbiased phosphoproteomic screen in axons undergoing TD, we discovered that some protein components of the MPS, including spectrin and adducin, were widely phosphorylated during TD (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by phosphoproteomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phosphorylations on the short C-terminal isoform of βΙΙ spectrin have been shown to reduce interactions with αΙΙ spectrin.
source: While the full impact of these phosphorylation sites on the MPS components remains to be investigated, analogous phosphorylations on the short C-terminal isoform of βΙΙ spectrin have been previously shown to reduce interactions with αΙΙ spectrin (Bignone et al., 2007) and thereby potentially inhibit the formation of the spectrin tetramer.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Bignone et al., 2007.

claim: Phosphorylation on adducin has been found to inhibit formation of spectrin-actin complexes and to affect spectrin localization.
source: Additionally, analogous phosphorylation on adducin, a protein known to enhance actin-spectrin interaction (Bennett and Baines, 2001), has been found to inhibit formation of spectrin-actin complexes and to affect spectrin localization (Matsuoka et al., 1996; Matsuoka et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Matsuoka et al., 1996; Matsuoka et al., 1998.

claim: Latrunculin A (LatA) binds actin monomers and prevents their polymerization.
source: We have previously shown that latrunculin A (LatA), which binds actin monomers and prevents their polymerization, disrupts the MPS in hippocampal neurons (Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge of LatA mechanism and citations to Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; Han et al., 2017.

claim: 3 hr incubation with LatA at a concentration of 20 µM was sufficient to completely disassemble the axonal MPS in DRG sensory neurons.
source: Consistent with our previous results, 3 hr incubation with LatA at a concentration of 20 µM was sufficient to completely disassemble the axonal MPS in DRG sensory neurons and this effect lasted for up to 12 hr after LatA removal (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This statement is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The effect of LatA on MPS disassembly lasted for up to 12 hr after LatA removal.
source: Consistent with our previous results, 3 hr incubation with LatA at a concentration of 20 µM was sufficient to completely disassemble the axonal MPS in DRG sensory neurons and this effect lasted for up to 12 hr after LatA removal (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This statement is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: During TD, DLK activity promotes phosphorylation and activation of c-Jun.
source: During TD, DLK activity promotes phosphorylation and activation of c-Jun (Xu et al., 2001; Ghosh et al., 2011; Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013; Larhammar et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2001; Ghosh et al., 2011; Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013; Larhammar et al., 2017.

claim: Activation of DLK during TD is associated with an increase in its apparent molecular weight on a western blot, reflective of TD-associated phosphorylations.
source: Activation of DLK during TD is associated with an increase in its apparent molecular weight on a western blot, reflective of TD-associated phosphorylations (Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013.

claim: An increase in the molecular weight of DLK in axons was observed upon LatA treatment.
source: Similar to the case of TD, we observed an increase in the molecular weight of DLK in axons upon LatA treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acute application of LatA strongly increased c-Jun phosphorylation.
source: In addition, we found that acute application of LatA strongly increased c-Jun phosphorylation and this effect was blocked by co-addition of a small molecule DLK inhibitor, GNE-3511, also similar to the case of TD (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The effect of LatA on c-Jun phosphorylation was blocked by co-addition of a small molecule DLK inhibitor, GNE-3511.
source: In addition, we found that acute application of LatA strongly increased c-Jun phosphorylation and this effect was blocked by co-addition of a small molecule DLK inhibitor, GNE-3511, also similar to the case of TD (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Acute disruption of actin and microtubules with cytochalasin D and nocodazole activates c-Jun in sensory axons.
source: Similar activation of c-Jun in sensory axons has been observed following acute disruption of actin and microtubules with cytochalasin D and nocodazole, respectively (Valakh et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Valakh et al., 2015.

claim: Retrograde signaling induces a transcriptional response in the cell body and the generation of an anterograde signal from the cell body to the axon that activates a latent pool of Caspase-3 in the axon.
source: It has been shown that retrograde signaling induces a transcriptional response in the cell body and the generation of an anterograde signal from the cell body to the axon that activates a latent pool of Caspase-3 in the axon.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Activation of axonal Caspase-3 triggers axon fragmentation.
source: Activation of axonal Caspase-3 in turn triggers axon fragmentation (Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016; Maor-Nof et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016; Maor-Nof et al., 2016.

claim: Physically isolating the axon from its cell body blocks the anterograde signaling and hence the TD-induced axonal Caspase-3 activation.
source: Indeed, physically isolating the axon from its cell body blocks the anterograde signaling and hence the TD-induced axonal Caspase-3 activation (Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2016.

claim: Application of LatA induced an increase in cleaved (activated) Caspase-3 in intact axons but not in axons severed from the cell bodies.
source: Notably, we found that application of LatA, like TD, induced an increase in cleaved (activated) Caspase-3 in intact axons but not in axons severed from the cell bodies (Figure 3E).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: An increase in Caspase-3-like enzymatic activity ('DEVDase') was observed in intact axons, but not in isolated axons, following LatA treatment.
source: In addition, we also observed an increase in Caspase-3-like enzymatic activity ('DEVDase') in intact axons, but not in isolated axons, in a way similar to TD, although the magnitude of TD-induced axonal DEVDase activity was consistently greater than that elicited by LatA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This statement is supported by DEVDase activity measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The magnitude of TD-induced axonal DEVDase activity was consistently greater than that elicited by LatA.
source: In addition, we also observed an increase in Caspase-3-like enzymatic activity ('DEVDase') in intact axons, but not in isolated axons, in a way similar to TD, although the magnitude of TD-induced axonal DEVDase activity was consistently greater than that elicited by LatA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This statement is supported by DEVDase activity measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Jasplakinolide (Jasp) is a toxin that promotes actin polymerization and thereby stabilizes F-actin.
source: We used Jasplakinolide (Jasp), a toxin that promotes actin polymerization and thereby stabilizes F-actin.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge of Jasplakinolide mechanism.

claim: Jasp effectively prevented disassembly of the MPS upon TD.
source: We repeated a time course of TD in the presence of Jasp and found that Jasp effectively prevented disassembly of the MPS upon TD (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This statement is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Actin stabilization can inhibit MPS disassembly and axon fragmentation.
source: This observation is consistent with the independent finding that actin stabilization can inhibit MPS disassembly and axon fragmentation (Unsain et al., 2018), but TD-induced retrograding signaling has not been studied in Unsain et al. (2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Unsain et al., 2018.

claim: Application of Jasp prevented the TD-induced rise in phosphorylated c-Jun (p-c-Jun).
source: To examine the effect of Jasp treatment on TD-induced retrograde signaling in axon degeneration, we examined phosphorylation of c-Jun and found that application of Jasp prevented the TD-induced rise in phosphorylated c-Jun (p-c-Jun) (Figure 4C,D), which is required in part for TD-induced degeneration (Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Phosphorylated c-Jun is required in part for TD-induced degeneration.
source: To examine the effect of Jasp treatment on TD-induced retrograde signaling in axon degeneration, we examined phosphorylation of c-Jun and found that application of Jasp prevented the TD-induced rise in phosphorylated c-Jun (p-c-Jun) (Figure 4C,D), which is required in part for TD-induced degeneration (Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2016.

claim: Jasp treatment prevented the TD-induced increase in the molecular weight of axonal DLK.
source: Likewise, Jasp treatment prevented the TD-induced increase in the molecular weight of axonal DLK (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), a proxy for DLK activation (Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Application of Jasp alone caused a small rise in the amount of detectable phosphorylated c-Jun-positive cells.
source: Interestingly, application of Jasp alone caused a small rise in the amount of detectable phosphorylated c-Jun-positive cells (Figure 4C,D), perhaps reflecting a low-level stress response initiated by inhibition of normal actin turnover.
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Knockdown of βII spectrin strongly protected axons from TD-induced degeneration.
source: Remarkably, we found that knockdown of βII spectrin strongly protected axons from TD-induced degeneration (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This statement is supported by axon degeneration assay data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: TD induces a rise in Caspase-3-like enzymatic activity ('DEVD-ase') in axons.
source: TD is known to induce a rise in Caspase-3-like enzymatic activity ('DEVD-ase') in axons (Simon et al., 2016), and we found that βII spectrin knockdown also blocked this rise in 'DEVD-ase' activity upon TD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2016.

claim: βII spectrin knockdown blocked the rise in 'DEVD-ase' activity upon TD.
source: TD is known to induce a rise in Caspase-3-like enzymatic activity ('DEVD-ase') in axons (Simon et al., 2016), and we found that βII spectrin knockdown also blocked this rise in 'DEVD-ase' activity upon TD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by DEVDase activity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genetic deletion of βII spectrin protected axons from degeneration following TD.
source: To further validate this finding, we established cultures from βII spectrin conditional knockout mice and infected these cultured neurons with Cre recombinase via lentiviral constructs to achieve a comparable removal of βII spectrin. Consistent with our shRNA knockdown results, genetic deletion of βII spectrin also protected axons from degeneration following TD (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by axon degeneration assay data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Loss of βII spectrin offered no appreciable protection against axon degeneration caused by direct activation of the apoptotic pathway (by ABT-737), direct damage to the mitochondria (by rotenone), or direct damage to the microtubule cytoskeleton (by vincristine).
source: In contrast to the protection observed against TD, loss of βII spectrin offered no appreciable protection against axon degeneration caused by direct activation of the apoptotic pathway (by the Bcl-2/Bcl-xL/Bcl-w antagonist ABT-737), or direct damage to the mitochondria (by rotenone) or to the microtubule cytoskeleton (by vincristine) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by axon degeneration assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: βII-spectrin knockdown inhibited the TD-induced rise in c-Jun mRNA.
source: We next examined activation of c-Jun and Foxo3a in wild type and βII-spectrin-deficient axons undergoing TD. We found that βII-spectrin knockdown inhibited the TD-induced rise in c-Jun mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), and prevented the increase in phosphorylated c-Jun (Figure 5E,F) and nuclear-localized Foxo3a (Figure 5G,H) upon TD, which are early events during axon degeneration signaling (Ghosh et al., 2011; Maor-Nof et al., 2016; Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: βII-spectrin knockdown prevented the increase in phosphorylated c-Jun upon TD.
source: We next examined activation of c-Jun and Foxo3a in wild type and βII-spectrin-deficient axons undergoing TD. We found that βII-spectrin knockdown inhibited the TD-induced rise in c-Jun mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), and prevented the increase in phosphorylated c-Jun (Figure 5E,F) and nuclear-localized Foxo3a (Figure 5G,H) upon TD, which are early events during axon degeneration signaling (Ghosh et al., 2011; Maor-Nof et al., 2016; Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: βII-spectrin knockdown prevented the increase in nuclear-localized Foxo3a upon TD.
source: We next examined activation of c-Jun and Foxo3a in wild type and βII-spectrin-deficient axons undergoing TD. We found that βII-spectrin knockdown inhibited the TD-induced rise in c-Jun mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), and prevented the increase in phosphorylated c-Jun (Figure 5E,F) and nuclear-localized Foxo3a (Figure 5G,H) upon TD, which are early events during axon degeneration signaling (Ghosh et al., 2011; Maor-Nof et al., 2016; Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: Activation of c-Jun and Foxo3a are early events during axon degeneration signaling.
source: We next examined activation of c-Jun and Foxo3a in wild type and βII-spectrin-deficient axons undergoing TD. We found that βII-spectrin knockdown inhibited the TD-induced rise in c-Jun mRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), and prevented the increase in phosphorylated c-Jun (Figure 5E,F) and nuclear-localized Foxo3a (Figure 5G,H) upon TD, which are early events during axon degeneration signaling (Ghosh et al., 2011; Maor-Nof et al., 2016; Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2011; Maor-Nof et al., 2016; Simon et al., 2016.

claim: The TD-induced activation of DLK was unaffected in βII-spectrin knockdown cultures.
source: Interestingly, the TD-induced activation of DLK, an earlier step in pro-degenerative retrograde signaling was unaffected in βII-spectrin knockdown cultures (Figure 5I).
evidence: This statement is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Loss of βII spectrin prevents the LatA-induced appearance of axonal DEVDase activity.
source: To examine a role for βII spectrin in pro-degenerative retrograde signaling more broadly, we applied LatA to βII-spectrin knockdown cultures and observed that loss of βII spectrin prevents the LatA-induced appearance of axonal DEVDase activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), although interestingly not the LatA-induced rise in phospho-c-Jun (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by DEVDase activity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Loss of βII spectrin does not prevent the LatA-induced rise in phospho-c-Jun.
source: To examine a role for βII spectrin in pro-degenerative retrograde signaling more broadly, we applied LatA to βII-spectrin knockdown cultures and observed that loss of βII spectrin prevents the LatA-induced appearance of axonal DEVDase activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), although interestingly not the LatA-induced rise in phospho-c-Jun (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: LatA treatment initiates an additional, less specific and βII-spectrin-independent signal to activate c-Jun, although this signal does not appear to lead to axon degeneration.
source: This is likely because LatA treatment, which disrupts all forms of F-actin, initiates an additional, less specific and βII-spectrin-independent signal to activate c-Jun, although this signal does not appear to lead to axon degeneration.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the observation that LatA activates c-Jun even in βII-spectrin depleted cells, but does not cause degeneration in these cells.

claim: The MPS is assembled early during axon development and remains a stable structure in mature, unstimulated neurons.
source: The membrane skeleton structure MPS, comprised of actin, spectrin and associated molecules, is assembled early during axon development and remains a stable structure in mature, unstimulated neurons (Zhong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zhong et al., 2014.

claim: MPS disassembly occurs without a change in the abundance of its component proteins.
source: However, unexpectedly, we find that MPS disassembly occurs without a change in the abundance of its component proteins.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MPS disassembly still proceeds normally in axons deficient in apoptotic pathway activation.
source: Additionally, the disassembly still proceeds normally in axons deficient in apoptotic pathway activation, suggesting that the disassembly happens upstream of Caspase-dependent proteolysis.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 2 showing MPS disassembly in Bcl-xL overexpressing and Bax knockout axons.

claim: MPS disassembly is an early event in the TD-induced degeneration pathway, independent of Caspase-dependent proteolysis.
source: Together these findings indicate that MPS disassembly is an early event in the TD-induced degeneration pathway, independent of Caspase-dependent proteolysis.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the timing of MPS disassembly relative to caspase activation and protein degradation.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of β spectrin has been reported to decrease membrane mechanical stability in erythrocytes.
source: We also observe extensive TD-induced phosphorylation on MPS components, spectrin and adducin. Increased phosphorylation of β spectrin has been reported to decrease membrane mechanical stability in erythrocytes (Manno et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Manno et al., 1995.

claim: MPS disassembly upon TD is prevented by pharmacologically stabilizing F-actin.
source: Furthermore, MPS disassembly upon TD is prevented by pharmacologically stabilizing F-actin, suggesting that TD-induced activation may activate one or more actin modifying enzymes, which may in turn contribute to driving the observed MPS structural changes.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4 showing Jasplakinolide prevents MPS disassembly.

claim: Loss or mutation of α/β spectrin family members from birth has profound consequences on nervous system development and integrity from C. elegans through mammals.
source: Loss or mutation of α/β spectrin family members from birth has profound consequences on nervous system development and integrity from C. elegans through mammals (Tang et al., 2003; Pielage et al., 2005; Hammarlund et al., 2007; Voas et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2013; Krieg et al., 2014; Krieg et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2017a; Huang et al., 2017b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2003; Pielage et al., 2005; Hammarlund et al., 2007; Voas et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2013; Krieg et al., 2014; Krieg et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2017a; Huang et al., 2017b.

claim: The depletion of βII spectrin protects axons from degeneration following TD, and this effect is downstream of the activation of DLK but upstream of c-Jun activation.
source: We observed that the depletion of βII spectrin protects axons from degeneration following TD, and that this effect is downstream of the activation of DLK but upstream of c-Jun activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 5 showing the effects of βII spectrin depletion on various markers.

claim: Loss of βII spectrin inhibits the pro-degenerative effects of acute F-actin breakdown by the actin depolymerization drug LatA.
source: In addition, loss of βII spectrin also inhibits the pro-degenerative effects of acute F-actin breakdown by the actin depolymerization drug LatA.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Beta-II spectrin depletion disrupts the MPS in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: It has been shown previously that beta-II spectrin depletion disrupts the MPS in cultured hippocampal neurons based on actin and adducin imaging (Zhong et al., 2014; Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zhong et al., 2014; Han et al., 2017.

claim: Beta-II spectrin knockdown led to substantial decrease in the abundance of some other MPS components, such as alpha-II spectrin and ankyrin-B.
source: However, we observed that beta-II spectrin knockdown led to substantial decrease in the abundance of some other MPS components, such as alpha-II spectrin and ankyrin-B, suggesting that the MPS is likely also disrupted in beta-II spectrin depleted DRG neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: TD-induced retrograde signaling involves loss of pro-survival Akt activity, culminating in activation of the downstream transcription factor Foxo3a.
source: TD-induced retrograde signaling involves at least two pathways in sensory axons. The first is loss of pro-survival Akt activity, culminating in activation of the downstream transcription factor Foxo3a (Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2016.

claim: TD-induced retrograde signaling involves a gain of pro-degenerative MAPK signaling, mediated by DLK, and culminating in phosphorylation and activation of the transcription factor c-Jun.
source: The second is a gain of pro-degenerative MAPK signaling, mediated by DLK, and culminating in phosphorylation and activation of the transcription factor c-Jun (Ghosh et al., 2011; Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013; Simon et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2011; Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013; Simon et al., 2016.

claim: In neurons lacking DLK, phosphorylation of c-Jun is blocked and activation of Foxo3a is strongly attenuated.
source: In neurons lacking DLK, phosphorylation of c-Jun is blocked and activation of Foxo3a is strongly attenuated (Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016), suggesting a crosstalk between these two pathways.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2011; Simon et al., 2016.

claim: Loss of βII spectrin does not block DLK activation following TD, but largely blocks phosphorylation of c-Jun and nuclear translocation of Foxo3a.
source: Loss of βII spectrin does not block DLK activation following TD, but largely blocks phosphorylation of c-Jun and nuclear translocation of Foxo3a, suggesting that βII spectrin is potentially involved in both pathways, but the extent to which βII spectrin interacts with each remains to be determined.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Actin stabilization by Jasp prevents MPS disassembly and occludes the somatic response to TD (i.e. inhibits activation of DLK and c-Jun).
source: Our data show that actin stabilization by Jasp prevents MPS disassembly and occludes the somatic response to TD (i.e. inhibits activation of DLK and c-Jun), suggesting that F-actin turnover is critical to this early phase of axon degeneration.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Acutely destabilizing actin with LatA largely phenocopies TD, inducing MPS disassembly and promoting retrograde signaling (i.e. activation of DLK and c-Jun), culminating in activation of the somatic pro-degenerative program.
source: Conversely, acutely destabilizing actin with LatA largely phenocopies TD, inducing MPS disassembly and promoting retrograde signaling (i.e. activation of DLK and c-Jun), culminating in activation of the somatic pro-degenerative program.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: βII spectrin depletion blocks the pro-degenerative effects of LatA-induced acute F-actin breakdown.
source: βII spectrin depletion blocks the pro-degenerative effects of LatA-induced acute F-actin breakdown.
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The MPS lacks a net polarity toward the distal axon or cell body.
source: The MPS lacks a net polarity toward the distal axon or cell body, so it is unlikely to act as a 'track' for pro-degenerative retrograde signal propagation.
evidence: This statement is based on the known structural organization of the MPS.

claim: The sub-membrane lattice structure of the MPS provides a mechanism for anchoring transmembrane proteins, likely in a way similar to the erythrocyte membrane skeleton.
source: The sub-membrane lattice structure of the MPS provides a mechanism for anchoring transmembrane proteins, likely in a way similar to the erythrocyte membrane skeleton (Hoover and Bryant, 2000; Bennett and Baines, 2001; Baines et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoover and Bryant, 2000; Bennett and Baines, 2001; Baines et al., 2014.

claim: Some functional membrane proteins are organized into periodic distributions along the axons by the MPS.
source: Indeed, some functional membrane proteins are organized into periodic distributions along the axons by the MPS (Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; D'Este et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014; D'Este et al., 2015; D'Este et al., 2017.

claim: The MPS may sequester and thus functionally inactivate some pro-degenerative signaling molecules in healthy axons to prevent aberrant signaling, but also primes axons for degeneration by recruiting these molecules to the appropriate region of the axons.
source: It is thus possible that the MPS sequesters and thus functionally inactivates some pro-degenerative signaling molecules in healthy axons to prevent aberrant signaling, but also primes axons for degeneration by recruiting these molecules to the appropriate region of the axons.
evidence: This statement is a speculative model proposed by the authors to explain their findings.

claim: MPS disassembly might activate retrograde signaling by releasing pro-degenerative signaling molecules.
source: MPS disassembly might then activate retrograde signaling by releasing these signaling molecules.
evidence: This statement is a speculative model proposed by the authors to explain their findings.

claim: Inhibiting establishment of the MPS may lead to mislocalization of pro-degenerative signaling molecules, resulting in failure of retrograde signaling.
source: On the other hand, inhibiting establishment of the MPS may lead to mislocalization of these signaling molecules, resulting in failure of retrograde signaling.
evidence: This statement is a speculative model proposed by the authors to explain their findings.

claim: MPS breakdown during TD (or following LatA treatment) may produce a pool of soluble MPS components, such as spectrin and ankyrin, which could participate in retrograde trafficking.
source: Another possibility is that MPS breakdown during TD (or following LatA treatment) produces a pool of soluble MPS components, such as spectrin and ankyrin, which could participate in retrograde trafficking.
evidence: This statement is a speculative model proposed by the authors to explain their findings.

claim: Biochemical reconstitution of dynein-driven retrograde signaling in the axon has demonstrated a prominent role for PH domain-containing β spectrins, including βΙΙ spectrin, in bridging vesicular membranes to dynein-driven retrograde motors.
source: Of note, biochemical reconstitution of dynein-driven retrograde signaling in the axon has demonstrated a prominent role for PH domain-containing β spectrins, including βΙΙ spectrin, in bridging vesicular membranes to dynein-driven retrograde motors (Muresan et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Muresan et al., 2001.

claim: AnkB has been shown as a motor protein adaptor important for retrograde transport of multiple organelles, such as endosomes and mitochondria, in hippocampal neurons.
source: In addition, AnkB, which is associated with the MPS, has been shown as a motor protein adaptor important for retrograde transport of multiple organelles, such as endosomes and mitochondria, in hippocampal neurons (Lorenzo et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lorenzo et al., 2014.

claim: The disassembly of the MPS to free MPS components could promote the role of these proteins in retrograde transport, which might in turn facilitate retrograde signaling in TD-induced axon degeneration.
source: The disassembly of the MPS to free these MPS components could promote the role of these proteins in retrograde transport, which might in turn facilitate retrograde signaling in TD-induced axon degeneration.
evidence: This statement is a speculative model proposed by the authors to explain their findings.

claim: Pharmacological and genetic manipulations often perturb multiple cytoskeletons simultaneously and may induce transcriptional responses.
source: Finally, we note that it is difficult to disentangle the roles of different cytoskeleton structures due to their interactions and due to the fact that pharmacological and genetic manipulations often perturb multiple cytoskeletons simultaneously and may induce transcriptional responses (Massaro et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Massaro et al., 2009.

claim: The depletion of βΙΙ spectrin could affect microtubule structure and microtubule-dependent retrograde transport in addition to the structure of the MPS.
source: Similarly, the depletion of βΙΙ spectrin could also affect microtubule structure and microtubule-dependent retrograde transport in addition to the structure of the MPS (Qu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Qu et al., 2017.

claim: Other cytoskeleton structures may contribute to the observed effects on axon degeneration in addition to the MPS.
source: Accordingly, while our manipulations of F-actin and βΙΙ spectrin converge on the MPS, it is also possible that other cytoskeleton structures may contribute to the observed effects on axon degeneration.
evidence: This statement acknowledges limitations and alternative interpretations of the data.
